answers.label: Q.1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Knowledge, technology and ways of learning are changing fast all over the world, so India's education system also had to change to keep pace.
answers.solution: The phrase means that all over the world, knowledge is growing and changing very fast: new subjects, new technology and new ways of learning and working are coming up. To keep pace with this worldwide change, India needed a new education policy, so the Government approved the National Education Policy 2020 in place of the 34-year-old policy of 1986.

answers.label: Q.1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: Every child, from pre-school up to the secondary level, should be enrolled in school (100% Gross Enrollment Ratio by 2030).
answers.solution: Universalizing education from pre-school to secondary level means making school education available to every child, so that all children from the pre-school stage up to the secondary stage are in school. The policy aims at a 100% Gross Enrollment Ratio (GER) in schooling, and plans to reach this goal by 2030.

answers.label: Q.1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: By opening Indian higher education to foreign universities and by bringing in a four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate programme with several exit options (and making all colleges multidisciplinary by 2040).
answers.solution:
The policy will make India a global knowledge superpower in these ways:
1. It proposes to open Indian higher education to foreign universities, so that Indian students get education of a world standard.
2. It introduces a four-year multidisciplinary undergraduate programme with various exit options, so students can study many subjects together and leave with a certificate at different stages.
3. It also aims to make all universities and colleges multidisciplinary by 2040.
The passage says: 'Thus, this new policy will strive to make the country a global knowledge superpower.'

answers.label: Q.1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: Board exams of classes 10 and 12 will be made easier; they will test core competencies instead of memorisation of facts; every student may take the exam twice.
answers.solution:
Testing will change in three ways under this policy:
1. The board exams for classes 10 and 12 will be made easier.
2. The exams will test the core competencies (real understanding and skills) of students instead of mere memorisation of facts.
3. All students will be allowed to take the board exam twice.

answers.label: Q.1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Educational streams are the academic subjects studied in school (science, commerce, arts); vocational streams teach practical, job-related skills (starting from class 6 with an internship). The policy removes the sharp separation between them.
answers.solution: Educational (academic) streams are the regular school subjects such as science, commerce and humanities, which build knowledge for higher studies. Vocational streams train students in practical skills for a trade or a job. According to the passage, vocational education will begin in class 6 with an internship, and the policy aims to remove any severe separation between the two streams.

answers.label: Q.1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: Admission to foreign universities will make education costly.
answers.solution: NEP 2020 may make education expensive because it opens Indian higher education to foreign universities. Admission to these foreign universities will probably be costly, so the overall cost of education will rise.

answers.label: Q.1(g)
answers.finalAnswer: Without enough skilled teachers, the policy will face practical problems in being carried out, especially in elementary education.
answers.solution: There is already a lack of skilled teachers in elementary education. Because of this, the policy may face practical problems when it is put into action at the elementary level, since a good policy cannot work without good teachers to carry it out. So its success may be limited.

answers.label: Q.1(h)
answers.finalAnswer: Skilled teachers may leave Indian schools to work in the foreign universities (an exodus of teachers).
answers.solution:
The passage warns of an 'exodus of teachers'. When foreign universities open in India, they will attract our skilled teachers, who will move to those universities. So Indian schools, especially at the elementary level, may lose their best teachers, which makes the shortage of skilled teachers even worse.
(The question as printed is oddly worded, 'affected by the success of NEP2020'; the passage answers how the policy will affect skilled teachers.)

answers.label: Q.1(i)
answers.finalAnswer: Its implementation.
answers.solution: The one factor that will truly determine the success of NEP 2020 is its proper implementation. The passage says: 'the implementation of this policy will greatly determine its success.'

answers.label: Q.1(j)
answers.finalAnswer: (i) unidisciplinary (single-discipline); (ii) influx
answers.solution:
(i) Multidisciplinary (covering many subjects): antonym unidisciplinary (or monodisciplinary, single-subject).
(ii) Exodus (a mass departure of people): antonym influx (a mass arrival).

answers.label: Q.2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Holding the poem up to the light like a colour slide; tying the poem to a chair and beating it with a hose.
answers.solution:
Two images that stand out:
1. Holding a poem up to the light 'like a color slide', which shows looking at a poem gently to see its colours and beauty.
2. Students who 'tie the poem to a chair with rope' and beat it 'with a hose', which shows them forcing a meaning out of the poem.
(Other images in the poem, such as a mouse probing its way out, feeling the walls of the poem's room for a light switch, or waterskiing across the poem's surface, are also correct answers.)

answers.label: Q.2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: Amusement mixed with sadness (sympathy for the teacher's frustration), because the playful images of enjoying a poem end in the violent image of students torturing it.
answers.solution: The poem makes me feel amused at first and then a little sad. The first part is playful and full of fun images (a mouse in a maze, waterskiing across a poem), so I smile. But the ending, where students tie the poem to a chair and beat it with a hose, shows the poet's frustration. I feel sorry that students miss the joy of poetry because they only hunt for its 'real meaning'.

answers.label: Q.2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Simile: 'hold it up to the light / like a color slide'; Metaphor/personification: 'tie the poem to a chair with rope / and torture a confession out of it'
answers.solution:
1. Simile: 'and hold it up to the light / like a color slide'. The poem is compared to a colour slide using 'like'.
2. Personification (an extended metaphor): 'tie the poem to a chair with rope / and torture a confession out of it'. The poem is treated like a prisoner who can be tortured and made to confess.
(Other correct answers: metaphor in 'press an ear against its hive', where the poem is a beehive; metaphor in 'walk inside the poem's room'.)

answers.label: Q.2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: A poem should be explored and enjoyed freely, not forced or over-analysed to find one fixed meaning.
answers.solution:
The theme of the poem is the right way to read poetry. The poet, a teacher, wants students to explore a poem with curiosity and enjoy it, as one looks at a slide, listens to a hive or waterskis across a lake. But the students only want to force out its 'real meaning', as if questioning a prisoner. The contrast between the playful first part and the violent ending shows that over-analysis kills the pleasure of a poem.
(The question is misprinted as 'What do you they think'; it means 'What do you think'.)

answers.label: Q.2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Forcing a fixed hidden meaning out of the poem by harsh over-analysis, as a prisoner is forced to confess.
answers.solution: To 'torture a confession' out of the poem means to force the poem to give up one hidden meaning by analysing it harshly, just as a cruel questioner forces a prisoner to confess. The students do not enjoy the poem; they only try to squeeze out 'what it really means'.

answers.label: Q.2(f)
answers.finalAnswer: To explore, experience and enjoy the poem freely, not just to find out what it really means.
answers.solution: According to the poet, the real goal of reading poetry is to experience and enjoy the poem: to look at it, listen to it, explore it and have fun with it, as in waterskiing across its surface. It is not to force one 'real meaning' out of it.

answers.label: Q.3
answers.solution:
Mangalam Vihar Colony
Kolkata
17 November 2022

The Editor
The Hindu
Chennai

Subject: Commercialisation of our festivals

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to express my deep concern about the growing commercialisation of the festivals we celebrate in our country.

Festivals were once times of prayer, family bonding and simple joy. Today they have turned into shopping seasons. Weeks before Diwali, Durga Puja, Eid or Christmas, television, newspapers and mobile phones are flooded with advertisements urging us to buy costly gifts, clothes and gadgets. Many families feel forced to spend beyond their means, and poor families feel left out. Puja committees compete over the size of pandals and the money from sponsors instead of devotion. Loud music, huge hoardings and firecrackers also harm our environment.

In this race to spend, the real meaning of each festival is being lost. Many children now link Diwali only with gifts and sales, and not with the victory of good over evil or with sharing sweets with neighbours.

I request citizens to celebrate with simplicity, to buy from local artisans, and to give time rather than money to their loved ones. Schools and community groups can remind us of the true message of each festival. Only then will our festivals keep their sanctity.

I hope this letter makes your readers think.

Yours faithfully,
Shalini
Mangalam Vihar Colony, Kolkata

answers.label: Q.4
answers.solution:
Global Citizens and Proud Indians

Some people feel that schools today teach students to be global citizens instead of building love for the nation. I do not fully agree with this view.

It is true that schools now teach us about climate change, world cultures, foreign languages and the United Nations. We use the internet to talk to students in other countries. This is important, because the problems of today, like pollution and pandemics, do not stop at borders. A child who understands the world will grow into a wiser and kinder adult.

However, being a global citizen does not mean forgetting our own country. In my school, we still sing the national anthem every morning, celebrate Independence Day and Republic Day, and learn about our freedom fighters and our Constitution. Learning about the world actually makes us more proud of India's rich culture, because we can compare and see its value.

Schools must keep a balance. They should teach us to respect all people while loving and serving our motherland. A true nationalist today is one who helps India stand tall in the world. So global citizenship and nationalism are not enemies; they are partners.

(about 195 words)

answers.label: Q.5
answers.solution:
Anxiety Among Children
By Salil, Class VIII

Most people think childhood is a carefree time. Yet many children today feel worried and nervous almost every day. This feeling, called anxiety, is a growing problem in our schools and homes.

Causes
The biggest cause is pressure to do well. Children face tests, tuition classes and competitive exams from a young age, and parents often compare their marks with those of others. Social media adds to the stress, because children compare their looks and lives with what they see online. Bullying, family problems and too little sleep also make children anxious.

Signs
An anxious child may have headaches or stomach aches, find it hard to sleep, lose interest in games, become irritable or keep quiet. Some children fear going to school at all.

What we can do
First, children must be able to talk freely. Parents and teachers should listen without scolding. Second, every child needs time to play, exercise and rest; sport, music and hobbies are natural stress-busters. Third, screen time should be limited, especially before bed. Schools can hold counselling sessions and teach simple breathing and relaxation exercises. Most importantly, adults should praise effort, not only marks, and remind children that one bad result is not the end of the world.

Conclusion
Anxiety is not a weakness, and it can be managed. With love, understanding and a healthy routine, we can help every child grow up confident and happy. Let us make our school a place where no child has to worry alone.

answers.label: Q.6
answers.solution:
Popular Culture and Global Citizenship

Today young people across India sing K-pop songs, watch Korean dramas and learn a few Korean words. Some elders worry about this, but popular culture can actually help us become good global citizens. Music, films, food, fashion and sports travel across the world and introduce us to the way other people live and think. When a teenager in Kolkata enjoys a band from Seoul, he learns to respect a culture very different from his own. Fans from many countries meet online, share their interests and become friends, which builds understanding and breaks down prejudice. At the same time, our own Bollywood songs, yoga and cricket reach young people abroad. A global citizen is someone who respects all cultures while staying proud of his own. If we enjoy popular culture wisely, it can join the world together.

(about 145 words)

answers.label: Q.7
answers.solution:
Wheels of Courage

The gym hall echoed with the squeak of wheels and the thud of a bouncing ball. Rohan gripped the orange basketball with both hands, his eyes fixed on the hoop. Around him, his friends spun their wheelchairs quickly, calling for a pass.

Two years ago, a road accident had taken away the use of Rohan's legs. For months he sat at home, sad and silent, sure that he would never play a game again. Then his physiotherapist told him about a wheelchair basketball club at the community sports centre. Rohan did not want to go, but his mother pushed him gently through the door.

That first day changed everything. He saw boys like him racing across the court, turning sharply and shooting with great skill. Nobody pitied anyone. They laughed, argued over fouls and cheered every basket. Their coach said, 'Your chair is not a cage. It is your pair of legs on the court.'

Now, in the final match of the inter-club tournament, the score was tied with seconds left. Rohan's teammate Arjun, in the blue chair behind him, shouted, 'Take the shot!' Rohan pushed hard on his wheels, stopped, balanced and threw. The ball curved through the air and dropped through the net.

The hall burst into cheers. His teammates crowded round, slapping his back. Rohan smiled the widest smile of his life. He had learnt that a disability can limit the body, but never the spirit. With courage and friends beside him, there was nothing he could not do.

answers.label: Q.8
answers.finalAnswer: (iii); (iii); (iv); (i); (ii)
answers.solution:
(a) Error in part (iii): after 'one of the least important', the noun must be plural. Correct: 'She is one of the least important persons in the office.'
(b) Error in part (iii): 'Hardly' is followed by 'when', not 'than'. Correct: 'Hardly had the teacher left the room when the pupils started enjoying.'
(c) No error (iv). 'The then Chairman' (the Chairman at that time) is correct, and the sentence is complete.
(d) Error in part (i): before a gerund we use the possessive form. Correct: 'Her walking hurriedly meant that she was in a raging rush.'
(e) Error in part (ii): 'want' is followed by the infinitive. Correct: 'he did not want to take action without listening to the reporter's version.'
(As printed, the part labels are misnumbered in (a) and (b), for example 'no error' is labelled (ii) in (a); the answers above use the intended numbering (i), (ii), (iii), (iv). In (e) 'reporters' also needs an apostrophe, 'reporter's', but the main grammar error is in part (ii).)

answers.label: Q.9
answers.finalAnswer: (i) Selfish; (ii) Frequently; (iii) Satiety; (iv) in: in: of; (iii) Torrential; (iv) Rubric; (i) Gender Dynamics; (iii) 1c:2a:3d:4b; (iv) Corrupted; (iv) Array; (ii) Expatia; (i) as the magic-bullet solution to disposing of otherwise; (ii) PSQR; (iii) asked us, "Where were all of you last night?"; (ii) simultaneous
answers.solution:
(a) (i) Selfish. 'But' shows a contrast with 'benevolent' (kind), so the opposite quality fits.
(b) (ii) Frequently. 'I visit my village frequently to see my aged grandparents.' An adverb of frequency placed after the object must be 'frequently'.
(c) Satiety (the third option, misprinted as a second '(iii)'). 'Satiety' is the noun meaning the state of being fully satisfied.
(d) (iv) in: in: of. 'A hockey tournament has been organized in Jaipur, one of the most affluent towns in Rajasthan and known as the pink city of the country.'
(e) (iii) Torrential. Torrential rains are very heavy rains that cause flash floods.
(f) (iv) Rubric. A rubric is a scoring guide for assessing students' work.
(g) (i) Gender Dynamics. It refers to how men and women behave and are treated in relation to each other.
(h) (iii) 1c:2a:3d:4b. Absolute = complete, Obsolete = archaic, Absolve = acquit, Obstinate = stubborn.
(i) (iv) Corrupted. 'Debased' means lowered in quality or morally corrupted.
(j) (iv) Array. An array is an impressive display or range of things.
(k) (ii) Expatia is wrongly spelt (the word is 'expatiate').
(l) (i) 'as the magic-bullet solution to disposing of otherwise'. We 'dispose of' waste.
(m) (ii) PSQR. Uranus married Gaia (P), had twelve children, the Titans (S), hid the children inside their mother after a prophecy (Q), and Gaia hated him for this (R).
(n) (iii) asked us, "Where were all of you last night?" A direct question ends with a question mark.
(o) (ii) simultaneous.
(As printed, (c) has two options labelled (iii), and in (h) options (i) and (iv) are identical; neither affects the answer.)

answers.label: Q.10
answers.finalAnswer: (ii); (i); (iii); (ii); (iii); (i); (ii); (iv); (iv); (iii)
answers.solution:
(a) (ii) won't be felt / will have been exhausted. 'Till next week' needs the future; 'by which time' needs the future perfect.
(b) (i) had learnt / started. The earlier past action takes the past perfect.
(c) (iii) have tried. 'For decades' up to now needs the present perfect.
(d) (ii) have estimated / is. Present perfect, and the picture is worth that amount now.
(e) (iii) will have / have finished. The exam is in the future; 'so far' needs the present perfect.
(f) (i) hasn't told / won't be coming.
(g) (ii) retired / had been. Past simple with 'by the time', past perfect for the earlier action.
(h) (iv) finished / had arrived.
(i) (iv) have visited / moved. 'Many times ever since' needs the present perfect; 'a year ago' needs the past simple.
(j) (iii) were / is. 'Many important people were imprisoned' in the past; the prison 'is visited' today.

answers.label: Q.11
answers.finalAnswer: for good; takes after; getting along; run across; get away
answers.solution:
(a) I'm leaving for good this time. ('for good' = forever)
(b) The child takes after his mother, not his father. ('take after' = resemble a parent)
(c) The new bird is getting along well with the other ones in the cage. ('get along' = have a friendly relationship)
(d) Let's run across the backyard and jump over the fence. ('run across' = cross by running; 'cut through' is also acceptable)
(e) The criminal wasn't able to get away with the murder. ('get away with' = escape punishment for)
(As printed, (a) and (d) can take more than one phrase; the answers above are the most natural ones.)

answers.label: Q.12
answers.finalAnswer: I was requested by Margaret not to forget to meet her the next day.; Though I warned Dev, he ignored me.; It makes no difference which chemical you put into the mixture first, the results will be the same.; Do you know who this pen belongs to?; This is the first time I have seen so many people in this building.; Most of the books had gone from the shelf when we left.
answers.solution:
1. I was requested by Margaret not to forget to meet her the next day.
2. Though I warned Dev, he ignored me.
3. It makes no difference which chemical you put into the mixture first; the results will be the same.
4. Do you know who this pen belongs to? (The instruction is misprinted 'Being'; it means 'Begin'. In an embedded question the word order becomes that of a statement.)
5. This is the first time I have seen so many people in this building.
6. Most of the books had gone from the shelf when we left. (Only a few remaining means most were no longer there.)

answers.label: Q.13
answers.finalAnswer: I told my teacher that I needed his help.; He told me that I was lucky.; The children told me that they would go out in the rain.; The teacher said that the school would remain closed the next day.
answers.solution:
(a) I told my teacher that I needed his help.
(b) He told me that I was lucky.
(c) The children told me that they would go out in the rain.
(d) The teacher said that the school would remain closed the next day.
Rules: 'said to' becomes 'told'; the present tense moves one step back into the past ('need' to 'needed', 'are' to 'was', 'will' to 'would'); pronouns change to fit the speaker; 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

answers.label: Q.14
answers.finalAnswer: tiny; careless; retail; produce; accidental
answers.solution:
(a) Immense (very large): tiny (or minute).
(b) Thorough (complete and careful): careless (or superficial).
(c) Wholesale (in large quantities): retail.
(d) Consume (use up): produce.
(e) Deliberate (done on purpose): accidental (or unintentional).
